To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the circadian rhythm in normal subjects is a progressive increase in pulmonary function, (2) the circadian variation in asthmatics is more pronounced than in normal subjects and (3) SO2 at a concentration of 0.50 ppm has no effect on the circadian variation of pulmonary function in normals, but it causes a small, immediate decrease of mid-expiratory flow in asthmatics which persists during the exposure.

the exposure to 0.5-ppm SO2 for 3 h does not result in any significant change of the pulmonary function of normals and that the exposure to this concentration of SO2 does result in a decrease of the pulmonary function in patients with a history or mild to moderate asthma, but that this change is less than that which is observed during a normal circadian rhythm.

0.5-ppm sulfur dioxide exposure for 3 h did not cause any significant change of the pulmonary function of healthy subjects, but did cause a small but statistically significant decrease of the mid-maximal expiatory flow rate (MMEF) in subjects with a history of asthma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of SO2 on respiratory function of normal subjects and asthmatic patients.
the effect of sulfur dioxide on the pulmonary function in normal subjects and in subjects with asthma.
the effect of SO2 on pulmonary function in normal and asthmatics and the possible role of SO2 as a trigger factor in asthma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present 0.5-ppm secondary standard is adequate to protect against acute effects of SO2 on the lung function of normals and asthmatics, but it is not adequate to protect against the circadian rhythm of the lung function of asthmatics.
SO2 at a concentration of 0.50 ppm for a period of 3 h did not cause a change of the circadian rhythm of the pulmonary function in normal subjects.
3 h of exposure to SO2 at the level of 0,5 ppm did not produce any significant effect on pulmonary function of either normal subjects or asthmatics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SO2 at a concentration of 0.50 ppm does not produce significant changes in pulmonary function in normal subjects.

SO2 at 0.5-ppm level has no significant effect on the respiratory function in normal subjects and that in mild to moderate asthmatics it results in a small but significant decrease of MMFR which is reversible.
the effects of 0.05 ppm SO2 for 3 h on the respiratory functions of normal and astmatics are small and of questionable clinical significance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the present secondary standard for SO2 of 0.50 ppm for 3h is not protective against the acute effects of this pollutant.
the circadian rhythm of lung function is more important than SO2 exposure in determining the response of normal subjects and asthmatics to a 3-h exposure to SO2 at the level of 0,5 ppm.
SO2 at 0.5ppm does not cause acute changes in the pulmonary function of normals.
